title: Verifier‑Assisted versus One‑Shot LLM Intent→Configuration: A Paired NetOpsTraceBench Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed NetOpsTraceBench, a paired comparison of a one‑shot NL→configuration pipeline and a verifier‑assisted generate–validate–repair pipeline on 1,200 intent→config episodes (study_id = rX4f7-1). Using gpt-5-mini, a deterministic NetOps validator, and Mininet‑style emulation, we applied a preregistered binary episode success rule (validator accepts final config AND emulator shows no availability degradation above tolerance AND no automatic rollback). Of 1,200 planned paired tasks we completed 1,199 pairs. Baseline success = 1,196/1,199 (0.9974979149); guarded success = 1,199/1,199 (1.0000000000). The paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0025020851 (95% bootstrap percentile CI [0.0000, 0.0058381985], bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10,000); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.25. Repair was invoked only three times. Under these controlled emulation and task‑corpus conditions we find no statistically significant advantage for the verifier‑assisted pipeline. We archive all artifacts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/results.json, execution/execution_manifest.json, execution/task_manifest.jsonl, execution/scoring/*.json) so that per‑cluster or sensitivity reanalyses can be reconstructed reproducibly.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are proposed as components that translate operator intent (natural language) into executable device configurations for network operations (NetOps). Surveys and system papers emphasize that operational reliability depends on the orchestration and assurance machinery (model + verifier + provenance + sandboxed execution) rather than on the base LLM alone [1,2]. Generate–validate–repair (verifier‑assisted) architectures are a canonical mitigation strategy: an LLM proposes a candidate, an automated verifier enforces syntactic and semantic constraints, and an automated repair loop iterates until verifier rules are satisfied [3–6]. However, paired, preregistered evidence comparing one‑shot generation against verifier‑assisted pipelines under emulator‑grounded rollback‑aware success rules is scarce.

We address this gap with NetOpsTraceBench: a preregistered, paired, emulator‑grounded study that asks: Can a reproducible, workflow‑centered benchmark of paired intent→config episodes produce an objective paired binary success metric that reliably distinguishes verifier‑assisted pipelines from one‑shot generation across two simulated topology clusters? Our contributions are: (1) a frozen preregistered experimental plan (rX4f7-1) and full execution artifacts; (2) a confirmatory paired analysis on 1,199 completed pairs using the requested model gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5; and (3) transparent reporting of an analytic deviation (binary outcomes → exact McNemar) and execution accounting explaining why the guarded pipeline rarely required repair.
sections.related_work: Recent surveys and system designs frame LLMs as components within broader AIOps/NetOps workflows and call for workflow‑centered evaluation (trace quality, validator interactions, rollback semantics) rather than isolated one‑shot QA tests [1,2,4]. Prior verifier‑assisted demonstrations in adjacent domains (NL→formal spec generation, topology compilation, and misconfiguration detection) show feasibility: automated verifiers reduce syntactic and some semantic errors by driving iterative repair, but reported gains depend on task selection and verifier strictness [5–10]. Empirical studies document LLM failure modes—hallucination, incorrect units/semantics, miscalibration, provenance loss, and prompt‑injection susceptibility—that motivate external verification and provenance linkers in NetOps settings [11–14]. These prior works motivate a reproducible, preregistered paired evaluation that archives provider traces, validator diagnostics, and emulator execution to make dependencies observable and analyzable.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: The study preregistration (NetOpsTraceBench, rX4f7-1; preregistration manifest SHA‑256 = 77abe8b4...) froze confirmatory hypotheses (H1–H3), inclusion/exclusion rules, seeds, stopping rules, and the primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The preregistration targeted 1,200 paired tasks (edge=600, core=600) and an MDE of 5 percentage points at α=0.05 given baseline≈0.70. The frozen analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1) computes an exact paired inference and a bootstrap CI per plan.

Task corpus and pipeline semantics: The benchmark used deterministically generated tasks (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) with schema‑specified initial_state, expected_final_state, required_sequence arrays, allowed_touched_fields, and declared difficulty levels. Per preregistration the design used a shared_initial_candidate generation semantics: for each task a single LLM candidate was produced and then evaluated in both conditions to isolate the verifier/repair intervention. Implementation details recorded in execution/model_configuration.json: requested_model = gpt-5-mini, max_output_tokens = 1500, hosted by adapter hosted_netops_gvr_v1; initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1; maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1; retrieval_augmented_generation = false.

Rationale for shared_initial_candidate (clarification requested by reviewers): We intentionally shared the same initial candidate across baseline and guarded conditions to isolate the causal effect of the verifier and the limited repair loop, eliminating inter‑generation variance as a confounder. This design improves internal validity for measuring the incremental value of verifier/repair, but it also reduces variability in initial candidates and therefore tends to lower repair invocation frequency relative to an independent‑generation design—an operational tradeoff we discuss below.

Deterministic validation, emulation, and success rule: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 performs canonical parsing, enforces workflow_policies (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields, minimum_active_in_groups), and emits structured diagnostics (validation_before/after, observed_touched_field_count, required_command_count, repair_applied). The preregistered binary episode success requires (1) validator acceptance of the final configuration (validation_after.valid == true), (2) emulator execution showing no availability degradation above the preregistered tolerance, and (3) no automatic rollback event during simulated execution. Inclusion/exclusion rules (contamination thresholds, unparsable outputs after one automated re‑execution, emulator measurement failures) were automated and logged.

Confirmatory analysis plan and executed test: The preregistration prespecified a paired nonparametric approach and bootstrap CI. Because outcomes were binary and concentrated in concordant pairs, the archived confirmatory analysis executed an exact McNemar two‑sided test on discordant counts and computed a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI using bootstrap_seed = 1729 and 10,000 resamples. All analysis code, seeds, and logs are archived.

Reviewer‑required disclosure regarding H3 (topology cluster breakdown): The preregistration included H3 (confirmatory: check sign consistency of paired difference across the two topology clusters). The archived confirmatory analysis artifacts do not contain per‑cluster contingency tables or per‑cluster inferential results; therefore H3 was not executed as a confirmatory subgroup test in the archived analysis. This is an explicit post‑preregistration analytic omission (no per‑cluster confirmatory outputs are present in analysis/*.csv or analysis/results.json). The raw artifacts necessary to reconstruct per‑cluster analyses (task manifests with per‑task metadata and the per‑episode scoring artifacts) are archived (execution/task_manifest.jsonl; execution/scoring/*.json); researchers can reconstruct per‑cluster contingency tables and run the preregistered subgroup checks from these artifacts without new model calls.
sections.results:
Execution and accounting: The run completed 2,398 of 2,400 planned episodes producing 1,199 complete paired observations (complete_pair_count = 1,199). Provider audit shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 1,203 (completed = 1,202; failed = 1) and stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 1,200, repair = 3. The small repair count indicates the guarded pipeline invoked the repair loop only three times under these task and validator settings.

Primary paired outcomes: The archived paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is: n11 = 1,196, n10 = 3, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Baseline_success_count = 1,196/1,199 = 0.9974979149291076; guarded_success_count = 1,199/1,199 = 1.0. Observed paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002502085070892446.

Inferential results and CI: The exact McNemar two‑sided test (on discordant counts n10=3, n01=0) yields p = 0.25. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (bootstrap_seed = 1729, 10,000 resamples) for the paired difference is [0.0000, 0.005838198498748957]. These numbers are archived in analysis/results.json and analysis/analysis_log.jsonl.

Missingness and exclusions: analysis/missingness_summary.csv records complete_pairs = 1,199; failed_baseline_episodes = 1; failed_guarded_episodes = 1; both_missing_pairs = 1. analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty (no automated contamination exclusions). The single dropped pair accounts for the reduction from the planned 1,200 pairs.

Repair and diagnostic patterns: Representative scoring artifacts (execution/scoring/task-00000*.json) illustrate that most shared_initial_candidate outputs were accepted by deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validation_after.valid = true, repair_applied = false). Declared task difficulty labels vary ("medium","hard","very_hard") in the task manifests, yet initial candidates frequently satisfied the validator—consistent with the low repair count recorded in the provider audit.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation: The paired inferential result shows no statistically significant advantage for the guarded pipeline under this corpus and validator configuration (p = 0.25; CI includes zero). Two artifact‑grounded explanations are supported. First, near‑ceiling baseline performance (≈99.75%) left minimal headroom; the preregistered MDE (5 pp) assumed a much lower baseline, so the run was not powered to detect the observed ≈0.25 pp improvement. The discordant counts (n10=3, n01=0) quantify the limited signal.

Second, design choices materially affected repair frequency and measured gains. The shared_initial_candidate semantics isolates verifier effects (internal validity) but suppresses per‑condition generation variability and thus tends to reduce the number of candidate failures that would provoke repairs. Additionally, the deterministic task generator produced well‑specified synthetic examples and the deterministic validator accepted the majority of initial candidates. These combined factors—task clarity, validator configuration, and shared initial candidates—explain why repairs were rare and why the paired difference is small.

Threats to validity and externality: Internal validity is strong due to frozen seeds, deterministic task generation, and automated exclusion rules. Construct validity depends on whether the binary success rule (validator acceptance + emulator availability tolerance + no rollback) corresponds to operational correctness in production. External validity is limited: only the requested model family (gpt-5-mini) was used, the corpus is synthetic/consented, and Mininet‑style emulation may not capture vendor idiosyncrasies or routing convergence. Verifier strictness materially affects outcomes; different validator settings could increase repair invocations and change measured gains. Finally, H3 (topology‑cluster confirmatory breakdown) was not executed as a confirmatory subgroup in the archived analysis; per‑cluster reanalyses can be reconstructed from archived per‑episode artifacts if applied as exploratory checks.
sections.conclusion: NetOpsTraceBench (rX4f7-1) provides a fully archived, preregistered paired evaluation comparing one‑shot and verifier‑assisted NL→config pipelines in an emulator‑grounded setting. Under the supplied synthetic task corpus, deterministic validator configuration, and shared_initial_candidate semantics, baseline one‑shot generation achieved near‑ceiling success and the guarded pipeline produced an absolute improvement of ≈0.25 percentage points (paired difference = 0.0025020851) that is not statistically significant (exact McNemar p = 0.25; 95% bootstrap CI includes zero). The run’s artifacts show repair was invoked only three times. These results should not be interpreted as a general refutation of verifier value; instead they quantify how corpus design, shared‑generation semantics, and validator thresholds jointly determine when verifier scaffolding will be exercised and measurable. We archive all raw outputs, provider traces, validator traces, and analysis code to enable reproducible per‑cluster and sensitivity reanalyses without new model calls.

limitations: Single model family tested (gpt-5-mini); results do not imply generality across other LLMs or fine‑tuned variants.
Task corpus skew: synthetic/consented tasks yielded near‑ceiling baseline success (≈99.75%), limiting headroom and statistical power to detect practical improvements by guarded pipelines.

Emulator fidelity: Mininet‑style emulation and deterministic validators approximate production behavior but may not capture all deployment failure modes (routing convergence, vendor idiosyncrasies, transient telemetry).

Verifier configuration dependence: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 acceptance thresholds and parsing rules materially affect outcomes; different verifier strictness could change repair invocation rates and measured gains.

Analytic deviation documented: the preregistration specified a Wilcoxon signed‑rank paired procedure; the archived confirmatory analysis used an exact McNemar test because outcomes were binary. This deviation is recorded in the archived analysis artifacts and in the Disclosure Statement above.
Operational external validity: absence of heterogeneous vendor renderers, real production templates, and live rollouts constrain direct production generalization.
